<content>
1: # Sync Integration Comparison
2: 
3: This reference compares the **sync providers** available in Super Productivity: how each stores and syncs your data, which platforms they support, how authentication works, and whether optional encryption is available. Use it to choose a sync provider or to understand how your data moves between devices.
4: 
5: For an overview of how integrations work (issue providers and sync providers), see [[4.24-Integrations]]. For conflict handling, backup behavior, and where data is stored, see [[4.23-Managing-Your-Data]] and [[3.06-User-Data]]. For a comparison of **issue** providers (Jira, GitHub, etc.), see [[3.07-Issue-Integration-Comparison]].
6: 
7: ## What Sync Providers Do
8: 
9: Sync providers **synchronize your full Super Productivity data** (tasks, projects, tags, time tracking, settings, archives, and so on) between this app instance and a remote location or another device. They do **not** import issues from Jira, GitHub, or other issue trackers; those are handled by issue providers. All sync in the app is **local-first** and **operation-based**: your device holds the primary copy, and changes are sent as operations (or a sync file containing state and operations) to the remote side. You configure one sync provider at a time.
10: 
11: ## Comparison Summary
12: 
13: | Provider         | Platform     | Authentication                         | Optional encryption         | Typical use                                  |
14: | ---------------- | ------------ | -------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
15: | Nextcloud        | All          | Username, optional login, app password | Yes (client-side key)       | Nextcloud files sync                         |
16: | WebDAV           | All          | URL, username, password                | Yes (client-side key)       | ownCloud and other WebDAV servers            |
17: | Dropbox          | All          | OAuth 2.0 (no password stored)         | Yes (client-side key)       | Cloud backup, cross-device sync              |
18: | Local file       | Desktop only | None (folder path)                     | Yes (client-side key)       | Single-device local or network-folder backup |
19: | SuperSync (beta) | All          | URL, username/password or token        | Yes (E2E, server-supported) | Hosted or self-hosted (limited support)      |
20: 
21: **Note:** SuperSync is very new and is still in beta. Prefer Nextcloud, WebDAV, Dropbox, or local file for production use until SuperSync is stable.
22: 
23: **Encryption timing:** When you first enable a file-based provider (Nextcloud, WebDAV, Dropbox, OneDrive, or local file), you are offered the option to set an encryption password as part of the setup. If you do, the password is saved with the sync config, so the very first upload — and every upload after — is encrypted; nothing this device uploads leaves it unencrypted. Encryption stays optional: you can skip the prompt and enable, change, or disable it later from the sync settings.
24: 
25: **Downgrade protection:** When encryption is enabled for a file-based provider, the app rejects an unencrypted remote sync file instead of importing it or automatically turning encryption off. If you intentionally disabled encryption on another trusted device, change the encryption setting on this device deliberately before syncing again. Otherwise, leave encryption enabled and check the remote account or connection for unexpected changes.
26: 
27: **Newer file formats:** If a remote sync file uses a newer format than this app supports, sync stops and asks you to update. The app does not recover that file from an older backup.
28: 
29: **Changes waiting during sync:** If too many local changes accumulate while remote changes are being applied, a persistent message warns that those changes have not been saved yet. It closes when the waiting changes are saved. Its **Reload** action discards the waiting changes.
30: 
31: **Android Nextcloud/WebDAV upload timeouts:** An upload may finish on the server after the app times out. The app reports the timeout without immediately replaying the upload; a later sync checks the remote state.
32: 
33: **Uploads rejected repeatedly:** When a file-based upload is rejected because the remote file changed, the next sync downloads first and retries without notice. If uploads keep being rejected for several syncs in a row, the sync icon shows an error and a message appears once; unsynced changes stay on the device until an upload succeeds.
34: 
35: ## Per-Provider Details
36: 
37: ### Nextcloud
38: 
39: - **Compatible with:** Nextcloud files WebDAV.
40: - **Configuration:** Server URL, username, optional separate login name/email, app password, and sync folder path. The username is used in `/remote.php/dav/files/<username>/`; the optional login name/email is only for servers that authenticate with a different value.
41: - **Encryption:** Optional client-side encryption; you set an encryption key that is not sent to the server.
42: - **Platform:** Available on desktop (Electron), web, and mobile. In the browser, CORS can block WebDAV requests; the app may recommend the desktop version for reliable sync.
43: - **Concurrent writes:** Atomic conflict protection requires strong ETags and a server that honors `If-Match`. The app also checks the revision before uploading, but this is only best-effort protection on servers that ignore write preconditions or provide weak or missing ETags.
44: 
45: ### WebDAV
46: 
47: - **Compatible with:** Nextcloud, ownCloud, and any WebDAV-compatible server.
48: - **Configuration:** Base URL, username, password, and an optional sync folder path on the server.
49: - **Encryption:** Optional client-side encryption; you set an encryption key that is not sent to the server.
50: - **Platform:** Available on desktop (Electron), web, and mobile. In the browser, CORS can block WebDAV requests; the app may recommend the desktop version for reliable sync.
51: - **Concurrent writes:** Same as Nextcloud: atomic protection needs strong ETags and a server that honors `If-Match`. Servers that compress responses and add `-gzip`, `-br` or `-deflate` to the ETag (Apache `mod_deflate`/`mod_brotli` by default) do not accept these ETags in `If-Match`. On them the app checks the file content before uploading, and on ownCloud and Nextcloud it also uses their `OC-ETag` header to make the upload conditional; other such servers get only the best-effort check. To keep atomic protection with compression enabled, set `DeflateAlterETag NoChange` (Apache 2.4.58+) and, with `mod_brotli`, `BrotliAlterETag NoChange`.
52: - **Advanced recipes:** Some storage providers can be exposed as local WebDAV with external tools. For Proton Drive via rclone, see [[2.19-Sync-Proton-Drive-via-rclone]]. This is not a built-in Proton Drive provider.
53: 
54: ### Dropbox
55: 
56: - **Configuration:** OAuth 2.0; you sign in with your Dropbox account. No username/password for Dropbox is stored in the app; the app stores tokens after you authorize.
57: - **Encryption:** Optional client-side encryption; you set an encryption key. Data can be stored encrypted in your Dropbox so that only this app (with the key) can read it.
58: - **Platform:** Available on desktop, web, and mobile.
59: 
60: ### SuperSync (beta)
61: 
62: - **What it is:** A dedicated sync server designed for Super Productivity, used via its hosted instance or self-hosted. **Self-hosting is possible but support for it is limited;** see [[2.13-Run-with-Docker]] for the tested setup. **SuperSync is very new and is still in beta;** consider Nextcloud, WebDAV, Dropbox, or local file for production use until it is stable.
63: - **Configuration:** Server base URL, then either username/password or an access token; optional sync folder path. Optional **end-to-end encryption** can be enabled on the server side so that the server stores only encrypted data.
64: - **Encryption:** Optional; when enabled, the server supports E2E encryption. You manage the encryption key; the server does not see plain data.
65: - **Platform:** Available on desktop, web, and mobile. Sync uses the same operation-based model as other providers but talks directly to the SuperSync server (no intermediate file in a generic cloud folder).
66: - **Live tracking presence (experimental, opt-in):** Enable it under Sync settings → Advanced → **Show live tracking on other devices**. While the real-time connection is active, a device that tracks time shows up on your other devices — a small chip in the header (and a silent Android notification) names the device and task, and offers a Stop button that ends the session remotely. Devices are named by platform and OS by default (e.g. “Desktop (macOS)”, “Android”); to tell two same-OS desktops apart, give each one a name under **Name of this device on other devices** (shown once the option is enabled). Idle pauses show as “Paused” without a Stop button. This is a live mirror only: it is never persisted on the server (only a short-lived in-memory slot while your devices are connected), rides the existing connection (no extra connections), and is end-to-end encrypted whenever sync encryption is enabled. SuperSync only; other providers have no real-time channel.
67: - **Network interruptions:** Temporary connection drops are retried. If the request still fails, local changes stay on the device and sync can retry later.
68: - **Large backlogs:** Regular downloads process large backlogs in passes, saving progress after each pass and scheduling the next one automatically. Full-history recovery downloads still require the complete history within one pass.
69: - **Connected devices:** Sync settings → Advanced → **Show Connected Devices** lists the devices that have synced with the account recently (the 100 most recently active), with their platform, client ID and last sync time. Access to a SuperSync account is granted per account rather than per device — a single long-lived token, not one per device — so removing a single entry would not stop that device from syncing, and no per-device revocation is offered. Instead, **Sign out other devices** (in the same dialog) invalidates every token except a fresh one issued to the device you press it on: use it when a device is lost or sold. Signed-out devices stop syncing and need a newly issued token to reconnect; changes made on them while signed out are kept locally and upload after re-authenticating. Devices that stop syncing drop off the list automatically after the server's retention period.
70: 
71: ### Local File Sync
72: 
73: - **What it is:** Writes the sync file to a local or network-accessible folder (e.g. a shared drive or NAS).
74: - **Configuration:** Folder path only; no remote account.
75: - **Encryption:** Optional client-side encryption with a key you set.
76: - **Platform:** **Desktop (Electron) only.** Not available in the web app or mobile, because those environments cannot reliably access arbitrary local or network paths.
77: - **Important limitation:** Use this as a single-device backup target. Do not mirror the folder between devices with Syncthing, Resilio, cloud-drive clients, or similar tools: local filesystem access cannot atomically coordinate concurrent writers, so simultaneous syncs can overwrite each other. Use Nextcloud, WebDAV, Dropbox, or SuperSync for multi-device sync.
78: 
79: ## File Sync Format
80: 
81: A new, empty sync folder uses the v2 format (`sync-data.json`), so no device
82: needs Surgical sync to join it. Existing folders keep their format: a v2 folder
83: stays v2, and a folder that already uses v3 split files (`sync-ops.json` and its
84: referenced snapshot) stays v3.
85: 
86: **Surgical sync** (Sync settings → Advanced) is an explicit, one-way upgrade of a
87: folder to v3. If a device reports that the folder was upgraded to the split-file
88: format, turn on Surgical sync on that device. App versions before 18.14 have no
89: Surgical sync setting and cannot sync a v3 folder.
90: 
91: ## Choosing a Provider
92: 
93: - **Nextcloud** — Use if you already have Nextcloud and want the app to build the WebDAV files URL for you.
94: - **WebDAV** — Use if you have ownCloud or another WebDAV server, or if you need to provide the full WebDAV base URL yourself.
95: - **Dropbox** — Use for cloud-backed sync without running your own server; OAuth keeps account credentials out of the app config.
96: - **SuperSync (beta)** — Use when you want a dedicated sync service and optional server-side E2E encryption. Bear in mind it is very new and still in beta.
97: - **Local file** — Use on desktop for a single-device backup to a local or network folder (e.g. an external drive or NAS), not for a folder mirrored between devices.
98: 
99: Logical conflict resolution (e.g. when two devices change the same data) uses the same operation rules for all providers. Transport guarantees still differ: Local file is single-writer only, and WebDAV atomic write protection requires strong ETags and enforcement of write preconditions. See [[4.23-Managing-Your-Data]].
100: 
101: ### When Automatic Conflict Resolution Stops
102: 
103: Reordering notes, habits, boards or sections can resolve automatically alongside an in-place edit of a reordered item on another device: note text or lock, pinning a project note to Today or unpinning it, a section's title or expansion, habit settings (including disabling the habit), a habit's count for any day, or board configuration. Both devices keep the edit and converge on an order. Moving or deleting an item, competing reorders, pinning or unpinning a note while Today or a tag's notes are reordered on another device, and missing history needed to recover safely can still stop sync. Older app versions may also stop on these reorder conflicts.
104: 
105: Reordering issue-provider tabs can also resolve alongside integration settings edits, such as changing an Enabled switch or pinning a search on another device. The tab order and settings are preserved across provider kinds. Deleting a provider or making competing reorders can still stop sync.
106: 
107: If sync stops with `SYNC_MULTI_ENTITY_UNSUPPORTED`, choose **Resolve…** in the error message or start a manual sync to open the recovery dialog. Background retries do not open the dialog automatically.
108: 
109: - **Keep local** replaces the remote dataset with this device's data. Remote-only changes are lost.
110: - **Keep remote** replaces this device's dataset with the remote data. Unsynced local changes are lost.
111: - **Cancel** leaves the conflict unresolved and sync stopped.
112: 
113: For file-based sync, keep all devices updated when using **Keep local** or **Force overwrite**. Current clients retain the replacement boundary through later uploads so other devices load the replacement before its later changes. Older writers can omit that boundary, allowing an offline device to miss the replacement.
114: 
115: This is a recovery fallback; it does not fix the underlying overlapping changes, so the conflict can recur. These choices replace the entire dataset, not just the conflicting tasks. Export backups from devices with changes you want to preserve before choosing a version. Remote change counts and timestamps are shown as unknown when unavailable.
116:

120: - [[2.19-Sync-Proton-Drive-via-rclone]] — Advanced Proton Drive setup through rclone and WebDAV
121: - [[3.07-Issue-Integration-Comparison]] — Issue provider comparison
122: - [[4.23-Managing-Your-Data]] — Backups, import/export, and sync from a user perspective
123: - [[3.06-User-Data]] — Where data and backups are stored, sync behavior by platform

(End of file - total 123 lines)

lines.text: This reference compares the **sync providers** available in Super Productivity: how each stores and syncs your data, which platforms they support, how authentication works, and whether optional encryption is available. Use it to choose a sync provider or to understand how your data moves between devices.

For an overview of how integrations work (issue providers and sync providers), see [[4.24-Integrations]]. For conflict handling, backup behavior, and where data is stored, see [[4.23-Managing-Your-Data]] and [[3.06-User-Data]]. For a comparison of **issue** providers (Jira, GitHub, etc.), see [[3.07-Issue-Integration-Comparison]].

Sync providers **synchronize your full Super Productivity data** (tasks, projects, tags, time tracking, settings, archives, and so on) between this app instance and a remote location or another device. They do **not** import issues from Jira, GitHub, or other issue trackers; those are handled by issue providers. All sync in the app is **local-first** and **operation-based**: your device holds the primary copy, and changes are sent as operations (or a sync file containing state and operations) to the remote side. You configure one sync provider at a time.
| Provider         | Platform     | Authentication                         | Optional encryption         | Typical use                                  |
| Nextcloud        | All          | Username, optional login, app password | Yes (client-side key)       | Nextcloud files sync                         |
| WebDAV           | All          | URL, username, password                | Yes (client-side key)       | ownCloud and other WebDAV servers            |
| Dropbox          | All          | OAuth 2.0 (no password stored)         | Yes (client-side key)       | Cloud backup, cross-device sync              |
| Local file       | Desktop only | None (folder path)                     | Yes (client-side key)       | Single-device local or network-folder backup |
| SuperSync (beta) | All          | URL, username/password or token        | Yes (E2E, server-supported) | Hosted or self-hosted (limited support)      |
**Note:** SuperSync is very new and is still in beta. Prefer Nextcloud, WebDAV, Dropbox, or local file for production use until SuperSync is stable.

**Encryption timing:** When you first enable a file-based provider (Nextcloud, WebDAV, Dropbox, OneDrive, or local file), you are offered the option to set an encryption password as part of the setup. If you do, the password is saved with the sync config, so the very first upload — and every upload after — is encrypted; nothing this device uploads leaves it unencrypted. Encryption stays optional: you can skip the prompt and enable, change, or disable it later from the sync settings.

**Downgrade protection:** When encryption is enabled for a file-based provider, the app rejects an unencrypted remote sync file instead of importing it or automatically turning encryption off. If you intentionally disabled encryption on another trusted device, change the encryption setting on this device deliberately before syncing again. Otherwise, leave encryption enabled and check the remote account or connection for unexpected changes.
**Newer file formats:** If a remote sync file uses a newer format than this app supports, sync stops and asks you to update. The app does not recover that file from an older backup.

**Changes waiting during sync:** If too many local changes accumulate while remote changes are being applied, a persistent message warns that those changes have not been saved yet. It closes when the waiting changes are saved. Its **Reload** action discards the waiting changes.

**Android Nextcloud/WebDAV upload timeouts:** An upload may finish on the server after the app times out. The app reports the timeout without immediately replaying the upload; a later sync checks the remote state.

**Uploads rejected repeatedly:** When a file-based upload is rejected because the remote file changed, the next sync downloads first and retries without notice. If uploads keep being rejected for several syncs in a row, the sync icon shows an error and a message appears once; unsynced changes stay on the device until an upload succeeds.

- **Configuration:** Server URL, username, optional separate login name/email, app password, and sync folder path. The username is used in `/remote.php/dav/files/<username>/`; the optional login name/email is only for servers that authenticate with a different value.
- **Encryption:** Optional client-side encryption; you set an encryption key that is not sent to the server.
- **Platform:** Available on desktop (Electron), web, and mobile. In the browser, CORS can block WebDAV requests; the app may recommend the desktop version for reliable sync.

- **Concurrent writes:** Atomic conflict protection requires strong ETags and a server that honors `If-Match`. The app also checks the revision before uploading, but this is only best-effort protection on servers that ignore write preconditions or provide weak or missing ETags.
- **Compatible with:** Nextcloud, ownCloud, and any WebDAV-compatible server.
- **Configuration:** Base URL, username, password, and an optional sync folder path on the server.
- **Encryption:** Optional client-side encryption; you set an encryption key that is not sent to the server.
- **Platform:** Available on desktop (Electron), web, and mobile. In the browser, CORS can block WebDAV requests; the app may recommend the desktop version for reliable sync.

- **Concurrent writes:** Same as Nextcloud: atomic protection needs strong ETags and a server that honors `If-Match`. Servers that compress responses and add `-gzip`, `-br` or `-deflate` to the ETag (Apache `mod_deflate`/`mod_brotli` by default) do not accept these ETags in `If-Match`. On them the app checks the file content before uploading, and on ownCloud and Nextcloud it also uses their `OC-ETag` header to make the upload conditional; other such servers get only the best-effort check. To keep atomic protection with compression enabled, set `DeflateAlterETag NoChange` (Apache 2.4.58+) and, with `mod_brotli`, `BrotliAlterETag NoChange`.

- **Advanced recipes:** Some storage providers can be exposed as local WebDAV with external tools. For Proton Drive via rclone, see [[2.19-Sync-Proton-Drive-via-rclone]]. This is not a built-in Proton Drive provider.
- **Configuration:** OAuth 2.0; you sign in with your Dropbox account. No username/password for Dropbox is stored in the app; the app stores tokens after you authorize.
- **Encryption:** Optional client-side encryption; you set an encryption key. Data can be stored encrypted in your Dropbox so that only this app (with the key) can read it.
- **Platform:** Available on desktop, web, and mobile.

- **What it is:** A dedicated sync server designed for Super Productivity, used via its hosted instance or self-hosted. **Self-hosting is possible but support for it is limited;** see [[2.13-Run-with-Docker]] for the tested setup. **SuperSync is very new and is still in beta;** consider Nextcloud, WebDAV, Dropbox, or local file for production use until it is stable.

- **Configuration:** Server base URL, then either username/password or an access token; optional sync folder path. Optional **end-to-end encryption** can be enabled on the server side so that the server stores only encrypted data.
- **Encryption:** Optional; when enabled, the server supports E2E encryption. You manage the encryption key; the server does not see plain data.

- **Platform:** Available on desktop, web, and mobile. Sync uses the same operation-based model as other providers but talks directly to the SuperSync server (no intermediate file in a generic cloud folder).

- **Live tracking presence (experimental, opt-in):** Enable it under Sync settings → Advanced → **Show live tracking on other devices**. While the real-time connection is active, a device that tracks time shows up on your other devices — a small chip in the header (and a silent Android notification) names the device and task, and offers a Stop button that ends the session remotely. Devices are named by platform and OS by default (e.g. “Desktop (macOS)”, “Android”); to tell two same-OS desktops apart, give each one a name under **Name of this device on other devices** (shown once the option is enabled). Idle pauses show as “Paused” without a Stop button. This is a live mirror only: it is never persisted on the server (only a short-lived in-memory slot while your devices are connected), rides the existing connection (no extra connections), and is end-to-end encrypted whenever sync encryption is enabled. SuperSync only; other providers have no real-time channel.
- **Network interruptions:** Temporary connection drops are retried. If the request still fails, local changes stay on the device and sync can retry later.

- **Large backlogs:** Regular downloads process large backlogs in passes, saving progress after each pass and scheduling the next one automatically. Full-history recovery downloads still require the complete history within one pass.

- **Connected devices:** Sync settings → Advanced → **Show Connected Devices** lists the devices that have synced with the account recently (the 100 most recently active), with their platform, client ID and last sync time. Access to a SuperSync account is granted per account rather than per device — a single long-lived token, not one per device — so removing a single entry would not stop that device from syncing, and no per-device revocation is offered. Instead, **Sign out other devices** (in the same dialog) invalidates every token except a fresh one issued to the device you press it on: use it when a device is lost or sold. Signed-out devices stop syncing and need a newly issued token to reconnect; changes made on them while signed out are kept locally and upload after re-authenticating. Devices that stop syncing drop off the list automatically after the server's retention period.

- **Configuration:** Folder path only; no remote account.
- **Encryption:** Optional client-side encryption with a key you set.

- **Important limitation:** Use this as a single-device backup target. Do not mirror the folder between devices with Syncthing, Resilio, cloud-drive clients, or similar tools: local filesystem access cannot atomically coordinate concurrent writers, so simultaneous syncs can overwrite each other. Use Nextcloud, WebDAV, Dropbox, or SuperSync for multi-device sync.

1: # Issue Integration Comparison
2: 
3: This reference lists which capabilities each **issue provider** supports: issue import, status transitions, time tracking/worklog submission, comments, subtasks, attachments, filtering options, auto-import to backlog, story points, due dates, and other provider-specific behavior. Use it to compare providers or to see what to expect when you enable one.
4: 
5: For an overview of how integrations work and how to set them up, see [[4.24-Integrations]] and [[2.07-Manage-Task-Integrations]]. For a comparison of **sync** providers (WebDAV, Dropbox, SuperSync, local file), see [[3.08-Sync-Integration-Comparison]].
6: 
7: ## Core Capabilities (All Providers)
8: 
9: Every issue provider supports the same basic operations: checking that the integration is enabled, testing the connection, opening the issue in the external system, fetching an issue by ID, searching issues, and adding an issue as a task in the app. All providers also support refreshing already-imported tasks so that changes in the external system (title, status, etc.) are reflected locally. Each provider has a configurable **poll interval** (or none) for how often the app checks for updates. Beyond that, support for status transitions, worklogs, comments, subtasks, attachments, and filtering depends on the provider and the external API.
10: 
11: ## Feature Matrix Summary
12: 
13: | Provider        | Import | Status        | Worklog    | Comments | Subtasks | Attachments | Filtering            | Auto-import | Story pts | Due dates |
14: | --------------- | ------ | ------------- | ---------- | -------- | -------- | ----------- | -------------------- | ----------- | --------- | --------- |
15: | Jira            | Yes    | Yes           | Yes        | Yes      | Yes      | Yes         | JQL                  | Yes         | Yes       | —         |
16: | GitHub          | Yes    | No            | No         | Yes      | No       | No          | Repo, assignee       | Yes         | —         | —         |
17: | GitLab          | Yes    | No            | Deprecated | Yes      | No       | No          | Project, scope       | —           | Weight    | Yes       |
18: | Gitea           | Yes    | No            | No         | No       | No       | No          | Repo, scope, labels  | Up to 200   | —         | —         |
19: | OpenProject     | Yes    | Yes           | Yes        | No       | No       | Yes         | Scope, status        | —           | Yes       | Yes       |
20: | CalDAV          | Yes    | Config        | No         | No       | No       | No          | Category             | —           | —         | Yes       |
21: | Calendar (iCal) | Yes    | No            | No         | No       | No       | No          | Text search          | Today       | Duration  | Yes       |
22: | Redmine         | Yes    | No            | On done    | No       | No       | No          | Project, scope       | Last 100    | —         | —         |
23: | Trello          | Yes    | Config        | No         | No       | No       | Yes         | Board                | Yes         | Yes       | —         |
24: | Linear          | Yes    | Auto (state)  | No         | No       | No       | Yes         | Team, project        | Yes         | —         | —         |
25: | Azure DevOps    | Yes    | No            | No         | No       | No       | No          | Project, scope, WIQL | Config      | —         | Yes       |
26: | ClickUp         | Yes    | Auto (status) | No         | No       | Yes      | Yes         | Team                 | Yes         | —         | —         |
27: | Plainspace      | Yes    | Two-way       | No         | No       | No       | No          | Space                | Yes         | —         | Yes       |
28: | Nextcloud Deck  | Yes    | Config        | No         | No       | No       | No          | Board, stacks, user  | Yes         | —         | —         |
29: 
30: **Legend:** **Status** = configurable or automatic status transitions; **Worklog** = time tracking submission to the external system ("On done" = dialog when a task is completed); **Auto-import** = automatic import of new issues into backlog (or "Last 100" / "Today" where noted).
31: 
32: ## Per-Provider Details
33: 
34: ### 1. Jira
35: 
36: - **Issue import:** Full import with JQL search.
37: - **Status transitions:** Configurable workflows (e.g. Open → In Progress → Done).
38: - **Worklog:** Full worklog submission and time-spent tracking.
39: - **Comments:** Comment tracking and display.
40: - **Subtasks:** Subtask relationship tracking and import.
41: - **Attachments:** Attachment mapping and display.
42: - **Filtering:** JQL-based search; auto-import with custom JQL.
43: - **Story points:** Custom field support.
44: - **Assignment:** Re-assignment on task start; assignee update when marking done.
45: 
46: ### 2. GitHub
47: 
48: - **Issue import:** Issues and pull requests from repositories.
49: - **Status transitions:** Not supported (issues are read-only from the app).
50: - **Worklog:** Not supported.
51: - **Comments:** Comment tracking with optional filter by username.
52: - **Filtering:** Search within repo; backlog query; username-based comment filtering.
53: - **Auto-import:** Configurable backlog query.
54: 
55: ### 3. GitLab
56: 
57: - **Issue import:** Full import from projects (cloud or self-hosted).
58: - **Status transitions:** Not supported. Closing an issue in GitLab does not complete the linked task, and completing the task does not close the issue.
59: - **Worklog:** Previously supported; now deprecated.
60: - **Comments:** Comment tracking with optional filter by username.
61: - **Filtering:** Project-based; scope (All, Assigned, Created); custom filter parameters.
62: - **Story points:** Weight field mapping.
63: - **Due dates:** Due date support.
64: 
65: ### 4. Gitea
66: 
67: - **Issue import:** Issues from repositories (self-hosted).
68: - **Status transitions / Worklog / Comments / Subtasks / Attachments:** Not supported.
69: - **Filtering:** Repository-based; scope (All, Created by me, Assigned to me); optional comma-separated label allowlist (AND match) and denylist (NONE match), both applied client-side and supporting scoped labels (`scope/name`). Also works against Forgejo. The `labels=` query is still sent to the server as a coarse pre-filter, but Gitea's `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues` and `/repos/issues/search` endpoints disagree on AND vs OR semantics ([go-gitea/gitea#33509](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/issues/33509)), so the client filter is the source of truth.
70: - **Auto-import:** Up to 200 issues for the project (4 pages × up to 50 per page; subject to server-imposed per-page limits).
71: 
72: ### 5. OpenProject
73: 
74: - **Issue import:** Work packages with project filtering.
75: - **Status transitions:** Full support with configurable workflows.
76: - **Worklog:** Time entry submission with activity types.
77: - **Comments:** Not tracked.
78: - **Subtasks:** Not supported.
79: - **Attachments:** Attachment upload support.
80: - **Filtering:** Scope (e.g. created-by-me, assigned-to-me); status and username filtering.
81: - **Story points / Time estimates:** Story point field and estimated time parsing/display.
82: - **Due dates:** Start date support.
83: - **Progress:** Percentage-done updates.
84: 
85: ### 6. CalDAV
86: 
87: - **What it uses:** The app requests **VTODO** components only. It does **not** read or display VEVENTs (calendar events). If your calendar has both events and tasks, only the tasks (VTODO) appear in the app.
88: - **Authentication:** **Requires login** (username and password or equivalent) to the CalDAV server.
89: - **Issue import:** Task/todo import from CalDAV. Sub-tasks may optionally be imported along with parent. For already-imported VTODOs, completion status, title, and notes can each be configured as **off**, **pull only**, **push only**, or **both**. This lets completion changes pull from CalDAV, push back to it, or sync both ways. New top-level tasks added in the provider's default project can optionally be uploaded as new VTODOs (**Create a CalDAV task for each new task in the default project**, off by default; subtasks and repeating tasks stay local, and the category filter, if set, is added to the VTODO). Deleting a linked task can optionally delete its VTODO on the server too (**Delete the CalDAV task when the linked task is deleted**, off by default). Undo, or restoring the task from Recently deleted, within the undo period keeps the VTODO; a later restore does not bring it back.
90: - **Status transitions:** Supported when enabled in configuration.
91: - **Worklog / Comments / Subtasks / Attachments:** Not supported.
92: - **Filtering:** Category-based filtering.
93: - **Notes:** Task notes/description support.
94: - **Due dates:** Start date with time support.
95: - **Related tasks:** Task relationship tracking.
96: - **URL format:** For Nextcloud, use `https://<NC-URL>/remote.php/dav/calendars/<USER>/<CALENDAR_NAME>/` from **“Copy private link”** (or the CalDAV URL), not the subscription/export link. For Vikunja, use the principal URL shown in Vikunja's CalDAV settings, e.g. `https://<VIKUNJA-URL>/dav/principals/<USER>/`, and set the CalDAV resource to the project name or project ID. Items without a valid VTODO are skipped.
97: 
98: ### 7. Calendar (iCal)
99: 
100: - **What it uses:** The app parses **VEVENT** components only from an iCal feed. It does **not** use VTODO (tasks). Events must have a valid **start time** (DTSTART); otherwise they are skipped. All-day events (date-only start) are included.
101: - **Authentication:** **No login.** You only provide the calendar URL (subscription or export link).
102: - **Issue import:** Calendar events (VEVENT) from iCal URLs. Events appear in the Schedule/Planner; event description becomes the task note. **Completion and time/date changes are not synced back**—the feed is read-only from the app’s perspective; if you change the task in the app, the external calendar is not updated.
103: - **Status transitions / Worklog / Comments / Subtasks / Attachments:** Not supported.
104: - **Filtering:** Text-based search in event titles. Calendar provider settings can also apply optional case-insensitive include and exclude regular expressions to event titles. The include filter acts as an allowlist; the exclude filter is applied afterward.
105: - **Auto-import:** Current day events. Deleting an auto-imported event task keeps
106:   that event from being imported again; using **Undo** restores both the task and
107:   its auto-import eligibility.
108: - **Time estimates:** Event duration used as task time estimate.
109: - **Due dates:** Event start time (all-day or timed).
110: - **Descriptions:** Event description as task notes.
111: - **URL format (example Nextcloud):** Use the **“Copy subscription link”** so the URL is in the correct form, e.g. `https://<NC-URL>/remote.php/dav/public-calendars/<CALENDAR-ID>?export`. Paste this in the app under **“URL of the iCal source.”** Do **not** use the “Copy private link”—that format is for CalDAV, not iCal.
112: - **Platform note:** The **Disable in web or Android app** setting suppresses iCal requests in the browser and on Android, where WebView network restrictions can produce similar failures.
113: 
114: ### 8. Redmine
115: 
116: - **Issue import:** Issues from projects.
117: - **Worklog:** Optional. When enabled, marking a linked task (or each subtask) done opens a dialog that posts a time entry, with a Redmine activity, to the issue.
118: - **Status transitions / Comments / Subtasks / Attachments:** Not supported.
119: - **Filtering:** Project-based; scope (All, Created by me, Assigned to me); task search supports non-Latin subject matches and `#123` issue ids.
120: - **Auto-import:** Last 100 issues for the project.
121: 
122: ### 9. Trello
123: 
124: - **Issue import:** Cards from boards.
125: - **Card creation:** Supported when a default Trello list is configured.
126: - **Status transitions:** Configurable. Completing a linked task can archive its card, and reopening the task can restore the card.
127: - **Title:** Configurable field mapping. Title updates pull from Trello by default.
128: - **Worklog / Comments / Subtasks:** Not supported.
129: - **Attachments:** Attachment mapping and display.
130: - **Filtering:** Board-based filtering.
131: - **Story points:** Supported.
132: - **Auto-import:** Automatic card import to backlog.
133: 
134: ### 10. Linear
135: 
136: - **Issue import:** Issues with team/project filtering.
137: - **Status transitions:** Issues auto-marked as done based on state.
138: - **Worklog / Comments / Subtasks:** Not supported.
139: - **Attachments:** Attachment mapping and display.
140: - **Filtering:** Team and project-based.
141: - **Auto-import:** Automatic issue import to backlog.
142: 
143: ### 11. Azure DevOps
144: 
145: - **Issue import:** Work items from Azure DevOps Boards.
146: - **Status transitions / Worklog / Comments / Subtasks / Attachments:** Not supported.
147: - **Filtering:** Project-based; scope support (All, Created by me, Assigned to me); optional custom WIQL query for auto-import.
148: - **Auto-import:** Configurable automatic backlog import limit, up to 200 work items. An optional WIQL query can fully override the auto-import query (scope, state filter, and ordering), for example to filter by iteration path, area path, or work item type. When empty, scope-based filtering is used.
149: - **Due dates:** Due date, target date, or start date support.
150: 
151: ### 12. ClickUp
152: 
153: - **Issue import:** Tasks with team filtering.
154: - **Status transitions:** Tasks auto-marked as done based on status.
155: - **Worklog / Comments:** Not supported.
156: - **Subtasks:** Full subtask support and relationship tracking.
157: - **Attachments:** Attachment mapping and display.
158: - **Filtering:** Team-based.
159: - **Auto-import:** Automatic task import to backlog.
160: 
161: ### 13. Plainspace
162: 
163: Plainspace is Super Productivity's own **collaboration** layer (a shared workspace at [plainspace.org](https://plainspace.org)), so it behaves differently from the read-mostly issue trackers above. You connect a **Space** with a personal API token (`pat_…`), and the tasks **assigned to you** in that Space import into the bound project.
164: 
165: - **Issue import:** Tasks assigned to you in the connected Space. A **claim pool** in the work view also lists **unclaimed** tasks you can claim into your list.
166: - **Status transitions:** **Two-way done sync** — completing a task locally marks it done in Plainspace, and a task completed in Plainspace is marked done on the next poll.
167: - **Title & schedule:** **Pull only** — a rename or reschedule made in Plainspace pulls in on the next poll (`scheduledAt` → `dueWithTime`), but renaming or rescheduling the task locally is **not** pushed back. **Recurring** tasks are flagged in the claim pool and task panel; the Plainspace server advances the schedule to the next occurrence.
168: - **Recurring tasks:** A recurring Plainspace task stays **one** local task across all its occurrences — Plainspace keeps a single item and moves its schedule forward. Once the server has advanced to the next occurrence, the local task is reopened and rescheduled on the next poll; if you archived it in the meantime, it is restored from the archive as the next occurrence. Consequences worth knowing: notes and subtasks carry over, **completed subtasks stay completed** (only the parent reopens), **tracked time accumulates across all occurrences** rather than starting fresh (unlike Super Productivity's own repeating tasks), and the completed occurrence leaves no separate archive entry. Archiving does not stop a recurring task from coming back — end or unassign the repetition in Plainspace instead. Deleting it deletes the whole series in Plainspace, for everyone in the Space. Because tracked time accumulates across occurrences, avoid setting a **time estimate** on a recurring Plainspace task: it is compared against the accumulated total, so once the accumulated time reaches the estimate, a task without subtasks counts as zero remaining time in the planner and schedule on later occurrences. Per-day tracking (worklog, daily summary, time exports) stays correct either way.
169: - **What is stored where:** The task's **title**, **done state** and **scheduled time** are stored on the Plainspace host (plainspace.org, or your own host) and are visible to the Space's members; the share dialog says so before you link a Space. **Notes, subtasks, tracked time and estimates** stay in Super Productivity and are never sent to Plainspace.
170: - **Worklog / Comments / Subtasks / Attachments:** Not supported.
171: - **Filtering:** By Space (one provider instance per Space).
172: - **Auto-import:** Assigned tasks auto-import into the bound project's backlog; the poll interval is 5 minutes. A task that **leaves** your Plainspace list (unassigned or removed) stays in Super Productivity but no longer updates. Deleting it then removes only the local copy.
173: - **Connection problems:** If Plainspace **rejects the token** (it was revoked, or replaced because you created a new one — creating a token revokes your previous one), the provider's tab in the **issue panel** shows **Reconnect**. Pasting a new token there (or via **Use a different token** in the space picker) updates every Plainspace integration that used the replaced token; an integration with a different token (another host or account) keeps its own. While **offline** or while Plainspace is unreachable, nothing is shown and nothing changes locally: tasks are never treated as removed, and the next poll retries.
174: - **Inviting people:** The shared project's context menu has **Copy invite link**, also offered on the confirmation after sharing. It copies the Space's web address; Plainspace sends people who aren't members yet to the Space's join page (a private Space shows its private notice instead).
175: - **Sharing a project:** You can turn an existing local project into a shared Space from the **project context menu → Collaborate on Plainspace**, or via the **Collaborate on this project** toggle when creating a project. 176: - **Disconnecting the account:** On an unlinked project, open **Collaborate on Plainspace → Disconnect account** in the space picker. 177: 
178: ### 14. Nextcloud Deck
179: 
180: - **Issue import:** Cards from one Deck board.
181: - **Status transitions:** Configurable. Done state pulls from Deck by default; with two-way sync, completing a task marks the card done and can move it to a configured done stack.
182: - **Notes:** The card description pulls into task notes by default.
183: - **Worklog / Comments / Subtasks / Attachments:** Not supported.
184: - **Filtering:** Board-based; optional stack selection and "assigned to me" filter. Archived and done cards are skipped.
185: - **Title:** Optional template with `{CARD_TITLE}`, `{COLUMN}`, `{BOARD}`, `{ID}`, and `{LABELS}`.
186: - **Auto-import:** Open cards from the selected stacks import into the backlog.
187: 
188: ## Implementation Notes
189: 
190: - **Broadest feature set:** Jira and OpenProject support the most capabilities: configurable status transitions, worklog submission, and advanced filtering. OpenProject adds progress percentage and activity; Jira adds JQL, subtasks, and assignment handling.
191: - **Comment-focused:** GitHub and GitLab offer solid issue import and comment tracking (with optional username filtering) but do not support worklog submission; GitLab worklog support is deprecated.
192: - **Subtask support:** Besides Jira, only ClickUp supports full subtask import and relationship tracking among the listed providers.
193: - **Calendar-oriented:** CalDAV and Calendar (iCal) are geared toward calendar/todo and event integration (categories, event duration, today's events) rather than full issue-tracking features. 195: - **Collaboration vs. import:** Plainspace is collaboration-oriented — done state syncs both ways, title and schedule pull in from Plainspace, and you can share a local project as a shared Space. Other providers are primarily imports from external trackers, though some fields can be configured for two-way updates where supported, such as Trello card status and title.
196: 
197: Optional capabilities (e.g. subtasks, attachments, sending updates back to the external system) are implemented per provider depending on what the external API supports.

Use it to compare providers or to see what to expect when you enable one.

For an overview of how integrations work and how to set them up, see [[4.24-Integrations]] and [[2.07-Manage-Task-Integrations]]. For a comparison of **sync** providers (WebDAV, Dropbox, SuperSync, local file), see [[3.08-Sync-Integration-Comparison]].

Every issue provider supports the same basic operations: checking that the integration is enabled, testing the connection, opening the issue in the external system, fetching an issue by ID, searching issues, and adding an issue as a task in the app. All providers also support refreshing already-imported tasks so that changes in the external system (title, status, etc.) are reflected locally. Each provider has a configurable **poll interval** (or none) for how often the app checks for updates. Beyond that, support for status transitions, worklogs, comments, subtasks, attachments, and filtering depends on the provider and the external API.

| GitHub          | Yes    | No            | No         | Yes      | No       | No          | Repo, assignee       | Yes         | —         | —         |

1: # Web App Vs Desktop
2: 
3: This reference enumerates functional differences and limitations of the web app compared with the desktop (Electron) app. Most limitations stem from browser security (CORS, CSP, sandboxing) rather than intentional feature removal.
4: 
5: When the web app is embedded in another Electron application, it retains web app capabilities and limitations. Desktop features require Super Productivity's own desktop app.
6: 
7: ## Features Unavailable or Restricted in the Web App
8: 
9: ### Plugin System
10: 
11: Plugins that require Node.js execution (elevated permissions) are disabled in the web version. When such a plugin is loaded, the app shows a disabled placeholder with an error stating the plugin requires the desktop version.
12: 
13: Listed community plugins install with one click in the desktop app. The web app
14: links to their ZIP instead, which you then install by hand.
15: 
16: Plugins are not strongly sandboxed from the host app on either platform. See
17: [[2.21-Manage-Plugins]] before installing third-party code.
18: 
19: ### Calendar Integration
20: 
21: Calendar providers can be disabled for the web app or Android app via an `isDisabledForWebApp` flag to avoid CORS and WebView failures. When this flag is set and the app runs in a browser or Android WebView, calendar event requests return empty results instead of performing the HTTP request. The UI shows a prominent warning that calendar integration will likely not work in the browser or Android app and recommends downloading the desktop version.
22: 
23: ### Local File System
24: 
25: - **Automatic backups to file system:** Available only in Electron (desktop) and Android; not in the web browser.
26: - **Local file sync:** The web app cannot sync to local or network folders; that sync provider is not available in the browser.
27: 
28: ### Time Tracking
29: 
30: In the web version, time tracking only works while the app is open. Idle time tracking in the browser requires the Super Productivity Chrome Extension to be installed. Without the extension there is no idle detection, so a forgotten timer keeps running; while a task is tracked the browser tab title shows the time logged on it today and its name (for example `25m - Write report`), which keeps a running timer visible from a background tab.
31: 
32: ### App Updates
33: 
34: The web app updates itself through its service worker and prompts for a reload when a new version is deployed. The desktop app instead checks the GitHub releases API once a day and shows a dismissible notice linking to the download page (configurable via the Misc setting "Automatically check for new versions"; not present on Microsoft Store, Mac App Store, or Snap builds, which update through their stores).
35: 
36: ### URL Scheme Actions
37: 
38: The `create-task`/`complete-task` URL scheme actions (see [[3.01-API]]) rely on the app having a registered custom URL scheme, which Electron and the Capacitor iOS and Android builds have. Not available in the web (browser) build.
39: 
40: The same scheme also carries UI actions that just open something: `add-task` (the quick-add bar), `today` and `inbox`. On iOS and Android all three work, and both expose them as launcher shortcuts — long-press the app icon to get New Task, Today and Inbox (Home Screen quick actions on iOS, app shortcuts on Android 7.1 and later). On desktop only `add-task` is recognized, and there is no dock menu or jump list for these. The web app has no launcher shortcuts either.
41: 
42: ## Browser-Related Limitations
43: 
44: ### CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)
45: 
46: WebDAV sync and calendar integration are likely to fail in the browser due to CORS. The app detects CORS-related failures and can show localized messages suggesting the user check server configuration. The desktop and mobile (iOS/Android) apps issue these requests through a native HTTP layer and are not subject to browser CORS; the web app is. This is why CalDAV calendar sync (e.g. with iCloud) works in the desktop and mobile apps but typically fails in the web app, where the server does not send the required CORS headers.
47: 
48: ### WebCrypto API
49: 
50: The web app depends on modern browser support for:
51: 
52: - **Dropbox PKCE authentication:** Requires `window.crypto.getRandomValues` and `window.crypto.subtle.digest`.
53: - **Secure context:** WebCrypto (e.g. `crypto.subtle`) is only available in secure contexts (HTTPS). The app shows alerts when WebCrypto is unavailable or when run over non-HTTPS.
54: 
55: ### Multi-Tab Instance Prevention
56: 
57: The web version uses BroadcastChannel to prevent multiple tabs from running the app at once. If another tab already has the app open, the new tab shows a blocker message asking the user to close one of the tabs.
58: 
59: ## Storage, Memory, and Performance
60: 
61: ### Browser Storage Persistence
62: 
63: The web app requests persistent storage from the browser. If the request is denied, the user sees a warning that data may be lost. Denial is surfaced via a snack notification.
64: 
65: ### Storage Quota Monitoring
66: 
67: The app uses the Storage API to estimate usage and quota. When available space falls to 333 MiB or less, the user is alerted that disk space is low and the app may be affected.
68: 
69: ### IndexedDB Quota Exceeded
70: 
71: When IndexedDB quota is exceeded, the app triggers emergency compaction with reduced retention (24 hours instead of 7 days) and uses a circuit breaker to avoid infinite retry loops.
72: 
73: ### Service Worker
74: 
75: The web app registers a Service Worker for offline caching (PWA). This is disabled for Electron and Android. Background behavior is limited to what the browser's Service Worker API allows.
76: 
77: ## File Size and Upload Limits (Sync)
78: 
79: These limits are enforced by the sync server; they affect web users who sync:
80: 
81: - **Operation payloads:** 20 MB maximum.
82: - **Compressed operations:** 10 MB maximum.
83: - **Snapshots:** 30 MB compressed, 100 MB decompressed.
84: - **WebDAV:** 10 MB maximum for XML responses; 100 MB maximum for file content.
85: 
86: ## Time Tracking Button
87: 
88: In mobile layouts, the header's play button uses a flat icon appearance when time tracking is inactive. While tracking, it shows a raised pause button. This applies to mobile browsers as well as the Android and iOS apps.
89: 
90: ## Offline and Background Processing
91: 
92: ### Background Throttling
93: 
94: The desktop app disables background throttling for its window. The web app is subject to the browser's background tab throttling, which can affect timer accuracy and background task execution when the tab is in the background.
95: 
96: On Android, a Focus session's foreground service keeps its timer and task time while the app is in the background. If a Pomodoro or Countdown session ends while the app is in the background, returning to the app records the task time up to the session end; a Pomodoro then starts its break. If time tracking continues during breaks, the time after the session end is recorded too. With manual break start, the session keeps running in overtime and records all of the background time. If Android recreates the app screen while that service is still running, the app restores the session and task time. This recovery does not cover Android terminating the entire app process.
97: 
98: ### Reminders Set on Another Device
99: 
100: On iOS, a reminder for a task you scheduled on another device only arrives once the iPhone or iPad app has synced that task, which happens when you open the app. The app schedules reminders as local notifications while it is running; there is no background sync on iOS. After the app has synced, the reminder is scheduled on the device and fires even if you close the app again. On Android with SuperSync, a background worker picks up reminders from other devices without opening the app.
101: 
102: ### Offline Support
103: 
104: The web app uses a Service Worker (production builds) to cache assets for limited offline use. Full offline behavior is more limited than on desktop and Android. The app shows an offline banner when the network is unavailable.
105: 
106: ## Plugin and Integration Limitations (Web)
107: 
108: ### Plugin API in Iframes
109: 
110: Iframe plugins receive a filtered `window.PluginAPI` object injected into `index.html`.
111: The iframe can use the injected task/project/tag APIs, dialog and notification APIs,
112: navigation helpers, persistence helpers, registration helpers, counters, and action
113: dispatch. APIs not injected into the iframe are unavailable, even if they exist on the
114: host-side plugin bridge.
115: 
116: `executeNodeScript()` is proxied through the host bridge for iframe plugins when
117: the desktop app grants the plugin `nodeExecution` permission. Both built-in and
118: uploaded plugins may request it. Uploaded plugins receive a native warning that
119: their identity is unverified and that granting access permits full machine
120: access.
121: 
122: ### Iframe Boundary
123: 
124: Iframe plugins use a supported bridge, but it is not a security boundary:
125: 
126: - The iframe includes `allow-same-origin`, which is required for the packaged
127:   desktop UI.
128: - Same-origin iframe code can reach the parent directly. The filtered Plugin
129:   API `postMessage` bridge is the intended interface, not enforced isolation.
130: - Inline CSS, JavaScript, and small assets in `index.html` for portable iframe plugins. Arbitrary extra files from uploaded plugin ZIPs are not served to the iframe; external URLs depend on the app/runtime CSP.
131: 
132: ### Chrome Extension for Integrations
133: 
134: Jira integration and idle time tracking in the web version require the Super Productivity Chrome Extension to be installed.
135: 
136: For self-hosted Jira instances where the server is configured with appropriate CORS headers, the extension requirement can be bypassed: enable **Fetch Jira directly from the browser (bypass extension)** in the Jira advanced settings. When active, the app sends API requests directly from the browser instead of routing them through the extension. This option has no effect in the desktop app or on Android.
137: 
138: If the Jira API is reachable at a different host than the public issue links (e.g. an internal API endpoint vs. a public URL), set **Alternative host for Jira links** to the public host. That value is used only for constructing browser URLs in task details, not for API calls.
139: 
140: ## Native Features Not Available in the Web App
141: 
142: The web version does not have:
143: 
144: - Native file system access (open/save dialogs, automatic backups to disk).
145: - OS-level notifications (it uses the Web Notifications API instead).
146: - Window management (minimize to tray, global show/hide, custom title bar).
147: - System tray integration.
148: - Global keyboard shortcuts (only in-page shortcuts; desktop can register system-wide shortcuts).
149: 
150: Certain UI elements tied to these features are hidden in the web build via platform-specific CSS or logic.
151: 
152: ## Spell Checking
153: 
154: Spell checking (red underlines for misspelled words) is intentionally disabled in the desktop (Electron) app on every operating system. On Windows and Linux, Electron's spellchecker downloads Hunspell dictionaries from Google's CDN by default, which conflicts with the app's offline-first, zero-data-collection approach. On macOS, Electron uses the operating system's native spellchecker instead. The desktop app disables spell checking at startup on all platforms. The setting is reapplied on every launch, which is why editing Electron's internal `Preferences` file to re-enable it does not stick.
155: 
156: The web app is not affected: in the browser, the notes editor uses the browser's own spell checking. Task titles and other short inputs have spell checking turned off on all platforms, a deliberate choice — red squiggles in task titles were repeatedly reported as distracting (issues #2874 and #4040).
157: 
158: Re-enabling spell checking in the desktop app is not currently configurable. On Windows and Linux, avoiding Google's dictionary downloads would require shipping or self-hosting spellcheck dictionaries; macOS uses native spellchecking APIs. If spell checking matters to your workflow, please describe it in an issue.
159: 
160: ## Platform-Specific Availability
161: 
162: ### Task Completion on Touch Devices
163: 
164: On touch devices, the task context menu omits **Mark as completed** and
165: **Mark as not completed**. Use the task's completion button to change its status.
166: 
167: ### Side Navigation Menus on Touch Devices
168: 
169: On touch devices, side navigation rows have no `⋮` button. Long-press a row
170: (a project, tag, folder, Today, Inbox, or a view such as Planner) to open the
171: menu that right-click opens elsewhere. Keyboard and screen-reader users can
172: still reach the `⋮` button: it shows while it has focus.
173: 
174: ### Receive Shared Links and Text on iOS
175: 
176: In the native iOS app, choose **Super Productivity** from another app's share
177: sheet, review the link or text, and tap **Save**. Each share creates one new
178: Inbox task when you next open Super Productivity. The supplied title is used
179: when available; otherwise the title comes from the shared text. The complete
180: shared content is stored in the task's notes. Task titles are limited to 300
181: characters and shared text to 100,000 characters.
182: 
183: Capture works offline. Pending shares stay on the device until imported;
184: they sync as ordinary tasks after import. Photos and file attachments are not
185: supported. This share extension is part of the native iOS app, not the web app.
186: 
187: ### Receive Shared Links and Text on Android
188: 
189: In the native Android app, choose **Super Productivity** from another app's
190: share sheet. Each text or link share creates one new task, placed as if you had
191: added it in the view that was last open in the app:
192: 
193: - **A project:** the task goes into that project.
194: - **A tag:** the task goes into your default project (the Inbox unless changed)
195:   and gets that tag.
196: - **Today:** the task goes into your default project and is scheduled for today.
197: 
198: A snackbar (in English) confirms the new task. The shared subject or title is
199: used as the task title when the sending app provides one; otherwise a link
200: becomes a readable form of its URL and plain text uses its first line. Titles
201: longer than 150 characters are shortened. The title is stored literally: no
202: short syntax in a shared page title, such as `#tag`, `@date` or `+project`, is
203: applied (see [[3.04-Short-Syntax]]). The shared link or text is
204: attached to the task as an attachment; the task notes are left empty.
205: 
206: Capture works offline. A share that arrives while the app is not running
207: shows a short "Content received, creating task…" notice and is added while the
208: app starts; it may then go to your default project instead of the last view.
209: Empty shares are ignored. Only shared text and links are supported; shared
210: images and files are ignored. This share target is part of the native Android
211: app, not the web app.
212: 
213: ### Exact Reminder Timing on Android
214: 
215: On Android 12 and later, reminders fire on time only while **Alarms &
216: reminders** is allowed for Super Productivity in the system settings. Android 14
217: and later turn it off by default for new installs. While it is off, reminders
218: are still delivered but Android may delay them, and the schedule and deadline
219: dialogs show a note with an **Open settings** button next to the reminder
220: option. After you allow it, reminders that are already scheduled switch to exact
221: timing without restarting the app.
222: 
223: ### Donation and Contribution Links
224: 
225: The Support Us page and links that can lead to GitHub Sponsors are unavailable in native iOS and macOS desktop builds. They remain available in the web app, native Android, Windows desktop, and Linux desktop builds.
226: 
227: ## Documented Error Conditions (Web)
228: 
229: - **CORS errors:** WebDAV (and similar) sync may report CORS failures with localized messages suggesting server configuration checks.
230: - **WebCrypto unavailable:** Dropbox OAuth and other crypto-dependent features show alerts when WebCrypto is missing or not in a secure context.
231: - **Storage persistence denied:** A snack notification warns when the browser denies the persistent storage request.
232: - **Quota exceeded:** The app handles multiple quota-exceeded variants (e.g. Firefox `NS_ERROR_DOM_QUOTA_REACHED`, Safari code 22) and triggers emergency compaction.
233: 
234: ## Notes
235: 
236: - The project README describes the web version as "a bit limited" and recommends the desktop version for full functionality, especially for calendar, file system access, and plugin support.
237: - The Android app offers a "Connectivity-Free Mode" for fully offline use; the web app does not provide an equivalent.
238: - Some integration features in the browser depend on the Chrome extension to work around security limits.
239: 
240: For installation and download options, see [[2.01-Downloads and Install]]. For sync backends and limitations, see [[2.09-Configure-Sync-Backend]].

(End of file - total 240 lines)

1: # Task Attributes
2: 
3: Task attributes are the properties that define a task's characteristics, state, and relationships in Super Productivity. They are central because tasks are the primary entity the app is built around: time tracking, project management, scheduling, and synchronization all depend on these attributes. Understanding how attributes work helps you see how the different features fit together and why certain actions (for example, setting a due date or adding a tag) affect what you see in the Today View, Schedule, or project lists.
4: 
5: ## Core Vs Optional Attributes
6: 
7: Tasks need a minimal set of attributes to exist and function. Beyond that, optional attributes enable scheduling, categorization, reminders, and other workflows.
8: 
9: ### Core Attributes
10: 
11: Core attributes are required for basic task functionality:
12: 
13: - **Unique identifier** — Each task has an ID so the app can track it across lists, sync, and archive.
14: - **Title** — The task name or description you see in lists and views.
15: - **Project** — Every task belongs to exactly one project; the project links the task to a workspace and its settings. See [[4.06-Project-View]].
16: - **Time spent per day** — The app tracks how much time you have logged on each day so time tracking and reports stay accurate.
17: - **Completion status** — Whether the task is done or not; the app uses this to show active vs. completed tasks and to drive archiving.
18: - **Subtasks** — A task can have subtasks; the app stores the list of subtask IDs so parent and child tasks stay linked. See [[4.11-Subtasks]].
19: - **Created** — When the task was created, used for ordering and history.
20: - **Attachments** — File attachments associated with the task.
21: 
22: With only these, you can create tasks, log time, complete them, and organize them in projects. Everything else is optional.
23: 
24: ### Optional Attributes
25: 
26: Optional attributes add scheduling, categorization, and integration:
27: 
28: - **Due date and due time** — When the task is planned for; used by the [[4.04-Schedule-View]], [[4.03-Planner-View]], and [[4.01-The-Today-View]]. See [[2.05-Manage-Scheduled-Tasks]].
29: - **Tags** — Category labels for cross-cutting organization. See [[4.07-Tag-View]].
30: - **Priority** — An optional High, Medium, or Low marker, set from the task's context menu or for several selected tasks at once. Task lists can sort and filter by it. See [[4.07b-Tags_Ordinal-Priorities]] for using tags when you need more levels.
31: - **Parent task** — For subtasks, the link back to the parent so the app can show hierarchy and aggregate time or completion. See [[4.11-Subtasks]].
32: - **Reminder** — When to be notified; the app stores reminder settings and the scheduled time.
33: - **Repeat configuration** — For recurring tasks, the rule that defines how the task repeats. See [[4.13-Repeating-Tasks]].
34: - **Time estimate** — Planned duration for scheduling and remaining-work display. See [[4.08-Time-Estimates]].
35: - **Notes** — Additional text you attach to the task. See [[4.10-Task-Notes]].
36: - **Issue integration** — When a task is linked to an external issue (for example Jira or GitHub), the app stores the connection so it can sync and show issue data. See [[4.24-Integrations]] and [[2.07-Manage-Task-Integrations]].
37: 
38: You can use none, some, or all of these depending on how you work. Tasks can start simple and gain optional attributes as you schedule them, tag them, or add reminders.
39: 
40: ## Workflow Support
41: 
42: Task attributes support different workflows by combining in consistent ways.
43: 
44: ### Time Management
45: 
46: - **Time tracking** — Time spent per day is updated as you track; the app uses it for daily totals and review.
47: - **Estimates** — The time estimate attribute drives the Schedule timeline and remaining-work display.
48: - **Scheduling** — Due date and (optionally) due time place the task on a specific day or moment, so the Schedule and Today View can show when work is planned.
49: 
50: ### Organization
51: 
52: - **Projects** — The project attribute groups tasks into workspaces; every task has exactly one project.
53: - **Tags** — Tag attributes let you label tasks across projects for filtering and grouping.
54: - **Hierarchy** — Parent and subtask attributes define the parent-child structure so you can break work down and see aggregated progress.
55: 
56: ### Integration and Extras
57: 
58: - **Issue tracking** — Issue-related attributes connect the task to an external system so the app can sync and display issue data.
59: - **Reminders** — Reminder attributes store when and how you want to be notified.
60: - **Repetition** — The repeat configuration attribute defines how the task recurs.
61: 
62: ### The "Today" List and Due Date
63: 
64: The app treats "today" as a special time-based group: whether a task appears in the [[4.01-The-Today-View]] is determined by its **due date**, not by adding a tag to the task. You do not add a "today" tag; you set the task's due date to today. That keeps scheduling consistent: the same attribute (due date) drives the Planner, Schedule, and Today list, so moving a task to today or changing its date updates all of these in one place.
65: 
66: ## Lifecycle Evolution
67: 
68: Task attributes change as a task moves from creation through active work, scheduling, completion, and archive.
69: 
70: ### Creation
71: 
72: When you create a task, the app assigns core attributes: a unique ID, title, project, created timestamp, empty time spent, completion status false, and an empty list of subtasks and attachments. Optional attributes (due date, tags, estimate, etc.) are added only when you use those features.
73: 
74: ### Active Work
75: 
76: - Time tracking updates time spent per day as you log work.
77: - You may set or change the time estimate as you refine the plan.
78: - Adding subtasks updates the subtask list and parent link on the child; the parent's remaining time and completion can be derived from subtasks.
79: 
80: ### Scheduling
81: 
82: - Setting a due date (or due date and time) adds the scheduling attributes. The task then appears on the Schedule and Planner for that day.
83: - When the due date is today, the task also appears in the Today View; the app uses the due date as the single source of truth for "is this task for today?"
84: 
85: ### Completion
86: 
87: - Marking the task done sets completion status and records when it was completed.
88: - Parent tasks can update their aggregated state based on subtask completion.
89: - **Won't do** (task context menu) finishes the task without completing it: it moves the task to the done list, but shows a cross instead of a checkmark. It doesn't count as completed in metrics or summaries, doesn't close or log work on a linked issue, and a parent is only marked done automatically if at least one of its subtasks was actually completed. Reopening the task clears it, and completing it later counts as completed.
90: 
91: ### Archive
92: 
93: When tasks are archived, core attributes are preserved so the task remains identifiable and historical data (for example time spent) is kept. Some optional data (such as reminders) may be removed in the archive so stored data stays lean. The task is no longer in active lists but remains available for history and backup. See [[4.20-Task-Archiving]].
94: 
95: The flexibility of the attribute system allows tasks to start minimal and gain complexity only when you need scheduling, tags, or integration—all within the same data model.
96: 
97: ## Editing Dates and Times After the Fact (Backfilling)
98: 
99: Several dates and times on a task can be edited later, not only when the task is first set up. In the task detail panel, each value is a link that opens a date and time picker:
100: 
101: - **Created on** and **Completed on** — shown at the bottom of the panel; the picker allows any date and time, including dates in the past.
102: - **Deadline** — can also point to the past (a deadline that has already passed).
103: - **Scheduled due date / due time** — the schedule picker does not allow past dates, so a task cannot be scheduled into the past. See [[4.12-Scheduled-Tasks]].
104: - **Time estimate / logged time** — adjusted through the time estimate control. See [[4.08-Time-Estimates]].
105: 
106: A common use is **backfilling**: after migrating or importing data, or simply correcting records, edit the “Created on” and “Completed on” dates of finished tasks so that history and time tracking reflect when the work actually happened.
107: 
108: ## Related
109: 
110: - [[4.06-Project-View]] — How projects organize tasks (project attribute)
111: - [[4.07-Tag-View]] — How tags organize tasks (tag attributes)
112: - [[4.01-The-Today-View]] — How due date determines "today" (due date attribute)
113: - [[4.04-Schedule-View]] — How the Schedule uses due date, time, and estimates
114: - [[4.08-Time-Estimates]] — How the time estimate attribute supports planning
115: - [[2.05-Manage-Scheduled-Tasks]] — How to set due dates and times
116: - [[4.24-Integrations]] — How issue and sync providers work
117: - [[2.07-Manage-Task-Integrations]] — How to set up and use issue integration
118: - [[3.04-Short-Syntax]] — Quick ways to set estimates, due dates, and tags in task titles

(End of file - total 118 lines)
</content>

1: # Board View
2: 
3: A **board** provides a visual, column-based way to organize tasks. Boards let you view and organize tasks from different perspectives using configurable columns (like Kanban or an Eisenhower Matrix) without changing the underlying task data.
4: 
5: ## What Problem Boards Solve
6: 
7: Boards solve the problem of **visual task organization**. They provide flexible, filterable columns that let you see tasks organized in different ways—by status, priority, urgency, or any other criteria you configure—while keeping the same underlying tasks.
8: 
9: For example, you might have a Kanban board with "To Do", "In Progress", and "Done" columns, or an Eisenhower Matrix with "Urgent & Important", "Not Urgent & Important", "Urgent & Not Important", and "Not Urgent & Not Important" quadrants.
10: 
11: ## How Boards Work
12: 
13: Boards are made up of **panels** (columns). Each panel has:
14: 
15: - **Filters** that determine which tasks appear in that panel (by tags, completion status, scheduling, one or multiple projects, backlog status, etc.)
16: - **Ordering** that you control by dragging and dropping tasks within the panel
17: - **Automatic updates** that modify task properties when you move tasks between panels
18: 
19: ## Moving Tasks Between Columns
20: 
21: When you drag a task from one panel to another, the app automatically updates the task to match the target panel's configuration:
22: 
23: - **Tags** are added or removed based on the panel's tag filters
24: - **Completion status** is updated (marked done or undone) based on the panel's setting
25: - **Project assignment** is updated if the panel specifies a project
26: - **Scheduling** is updated (scheduled or unscheduled) based on the panel's setting
27: 
28: This means moving a task to a "Done" panel marks it complete, and moving it to a panel that requires certain tags adds those tags to the task.
29: 
30: ## Multiple Boards and Task Membership
31: 
32: Tasks can appear on **multiple boards simultaneously**. This works because:
33: 
34: - Each board panel independently filters tasks from active projects based on its criteria
35: - Tasks don't store which boards they belong to—membership is calculated dynamically
36: - Each panel maintains its own ordering, so a task can be in different positions on different boards
37: 
38: For example, a task might appear in the "Urgent" column of an Eisenhower Matrix board and also in the "In Progress" column of a Kanban board, with different positions in each.
39: 
40: Boards include tasks from projects that are hidden from the sidebar. Hidden projects are still active; only archived projects are removed from board task membership.
41: 
42: ## Boards Vs Projects Vs Tags
43: 
44: | Feature               | Boards                             | Projects                          | Tags                                   |
45: | --------------------- | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
46: | **Purpose**           | Visual organization with columns   | Task grouping and structure       | Cross-cutting categorization           |
47: | **Task Relationship** | Dynamic filtering-based membership | Direct assignment (required)      | Direct assignment (optional, multiple) |
48: | **Visual**            | Column-based layout                | Tree view in sidebar              | Badge display on tasks                 |
49: | **Persistence**       | Board configurations are saved     | Project data and task assignments | Tag data and task assignments          |
50: 
51: Boards provide a flexible visual layer on top of your existing task-project-tag structure. They let you create multiple simultaneous views of the same tasks without duplicating the underlying task data.
52: 
53: ## Default Boards
54: 
55: The app includes two default boards:
56: 
57: - **Eisenhower Matrix** — Organizes tasks by urgency and importance (4 quadrants)
58: - **Kanban** — Organizes tasks by workflow stage (To Do, In Progress, Done)
59: 
60: You can create custom boards with your own panels and filters to match your workflow.
61: 
62: ## Related
63: 
64: - [[4.06-Project-View]] — How projects provide structural organization
65: - [[4.07-Tag-View]] — How tags provide cross-cutting categorization
66: - [[4.01-The-Today-View]] — Today's task list
67: - [[4.03-Planner-View]] — Day-level planning
68: - [[4.04-Schedule-View]] — Time-based scheduling

(End of file - total 68 lines)
</content>
